Clean air laws cut the smoke. Rain washes the soot off, and lichen starts to grow back.

Peppered moths rest on tree bark by day. Most were pale with dark speckles, hard to see on bark covered in pale lichen.
Moth DNA dates the change that makes the dark form to around 1819: a jumping piece of DNA landed in a gene called cortex. One dark copy makes a dark moth.
A collector in Manchester caught the first recorded dark peppered moth.
Coal smoke darkened the bark with soot, and pollution killed many pale lichens. By the end of the 1800s, about 98 in 100 peppered moths near Manchester were dark.
Bernard Kettlewell released moths in polluted woods near Birmingham and clean woods in Dorset. Birds took more of whichever form stood out.
Britain's Clean Air Act made towns cut smoke. From the 1960s and 1970s on, the dark form fell steadily. Dark moths in Michigan, USA, rose and fell the same way.
Scientists agree that less soot mattered. How much returning lichen mattered is still argued: in Michigan the dark form fell even where lichen had not come back.
Michael Majerus watched 4,864 released moths in Cambridge. Birds ate more of the dark ones, enough to explain why the dark form is fading.
